title: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz
hook: a caliph of the ruling family who began his reforms with his own family's wealth

segments.voice: Yesterday: the dinar, words where a face had been. Your line was words instead of faces.

A lamp is burning on a desk in Damascus. A visitor comes in, and once the state's business is done, the talk turns to family news. The man at the desk reaches over, puts the lamp out, and lights a different one. The first lamp, he explains, burns oil paid for by the public treasury. This conversation is his own, so it gets his own lamp. That's a story people tell about Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, an Umayyad caliph. Whether or not it happened just that way, it shows what people remembered: a ruler who kept careful track of what was his and what belonged to everyone. Today: the caliph they called just.
screen: `A LAMP ON A DESK.` → `PUT OUT FOR A PRIVATE TALK.` → `WHAT IS MINE, WHAT IS EVERYONE'S.`

segments.voice: Start with another story people tell: the girl and the milk. The caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab is walking Medina by night. Through a wall he hears a mother tell her daughter to stretch the milk with water before selling it. The daughter says the caliph has forbidden that. The mother says the caliph can't see them. And the girl answers: if Umar does not see, the Lord of Umar sees. The story says Umar married her to his son. Her daughter's son was Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz. So he is the just grandson: the girl who wouldn't cheat in the dark was his grandmother, and the caliph who heard her was his forebear. Now the man himself. Born into the ruling family and raised in comfort, he was, the histories say, governor of Medina before he became caliph. When he took power, the reports say he started with his own house, returning lands and goods his family had taken unjustly, beginning with what he held himself. His wife Fatima, a caliph's daughter, is reported to have given her jewels to the treasury. He also ended something ugly. Under earlier Umayyad rulers, Ali ibn Abi Talib had been cursed from the pulpits. Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz stopped it, and the reports say the Friday sermon came to close with a verse instead, the one that begins, in Pickthall's translation, "Lo! Allah enjoineth justice and kindness." His rule was short. But some Sunni scholars later counted him with the rightly guided caliphs, calling him the fifth.
screen: `THE GIRL AND THE MILK.` · `HE STARTED WITH HIS OWN HOUSE.` · `THE CURSING STOPPED.` · then, large: `JUSTICE AND KINDNESS.`

segments.voice: Picture the two lamps on the desk, and name one thing in your life that is more than you need: a subscription, a second helping, an extra hour on a screen. If you pray, ask for contentment in your own words; if you don't, rest with the question of what is enough.
Umar. The Umayyad caliph remembered for justice and simple living, who returned what his own family had taken and ended the cursing from the pulpits. Today's word.
Your line: the just grandson. One lamp for the public, one for himself. Day nine hundred seven.

howItsDone: Muslims often tell stories of Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, such as the two lamps, when they talk about honest leadership and keeping public money apart from private use.

chat.says: Why do some call Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz the fifth rightly guided caliph?
options: He returned what his family took unjustly and stopped the cursing of Ali.
He was the fifth son of Umar ibn al-Khattab, so the title passed to him.
He conquered more land than the four caliphs before him put together.
chat.meaning: The reports say he started justice with his own house and ended the cursing of Ali; some Sunni scholars counted him the fifth.
